text: A popular open-air dance garden on the Boulevard du Montparnasse, haunt of students and grisettes in the 1820s and 30s. Courfeyrac's cure for Marius's gloom is the standard student one: go dancing.

Sceaux, a village a few miles south of Paris, held a famous Sunday dance in its park, reached by crowded carriages and carts. Grantaire's sneer that this is where 'all lost women' turn up reflects its reputation as a place of easy pleasure.

Candlemas, 2 February, was folk weather-day: if the sun shone, the bear went back into its den for six more weeks of winter (the origin of Groundhog Day). Mathieu Laensberg was the supposed author of a cheap almanac from Liège, full of such sayings. Hugo uses the rhyme to date the snow that falls on the Gorbeau house.

Hapgood's English for a slang name for the police (in French, 'les cognes'). The girls on the boulevard use it, and Marius only half understands; it is the first taste in this part of the book of the underworld's own language.

Writing false petitions to the rich under invented identities was a recognised Paris trade. Each letter here plays to its reader: a Spanish royalist exile for a legitimist marquise, an abandoned mother for a countess, a playwright for a shopkeeper with literary pretensions, a 'dramatic artist' for a churchgoer. The spelling mistakes repeated across all four give the game away.
quote: all four were written by the same hand

text: After France crushed the Spanish liberals in 1823 and restored Ferdinand VII, Spanish exiles of both camps drifted through Paris and appealed to French royalists for help. 'Legitimacy' was the royalist watchword: the right of the old dynasty against usurpers. A sham 'Don Alvarès' is calculated to touch a marquise who mourns the fallen Bourbons.

Under the July Monarchy only men paying at least 200 francs a year in direct taxes could vote: about 170,000 in a country of over thirty million. To sign oneself 'Elector' was a mark of solid bourgeois standing, which is why the letter-writer flatters a wholesale stocking merchant with it.

The Comédie-Française, the state theatre in the Rue de Richelieu, home of classical tragedy and comedy. Getting a play accepted there was the summit of a playwright's hopes; the begging 'man of letters' claims to have sent it a drama.

A parish church in the Rue Saint-Jacques, on the slope of the Latin Quarter south of the Luxembourg. The 'benevolent gentleman' who hears mass there every day is the old man the begging letter targets.
Light comic plays with popular songs set to well-known tunes; their refrains circulated in the streets like hit songs. The girl hums scraps of them as she prowls Marius's room.

term: 'J'ai faim, mon père. Pas de fricot.'
text: A mock-cheerful street rhyme: 'I'm hungry, father. No stew. I'm cold, mother. No knitting.' The jaunty tune and the grim words together are the girl's whole manner.
Slang names for a five-franc piece, the big silver coin. Five francs was several days' food for a family like this one, which is why the coin melts 'the avalanches of slang' in her head.
quote: Five francs! the shiner! a monarch!

text: Johann Kaspar Lavater, Swiss pastor whose books on physiognomy (1770s) claimed to read character in the face. Hugo borrows the idea for his portrait of Jondrette: vulture and pettifogger in one face.
quote: If Lavater had studied this visage

term: 'The Dream' and 'Maringo Austerlits Iena Wagramme Elot'
text: A cheap coloured print of Bonapartist sentiment: Napoleon in glory, and a sleeping child, Napoleon's son the King of Rome, whose crown a woman pushes away. The column lists Napoleon's victories, Marengo, Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram, Eylau, comically misspelled. The family who hang it call themselves 'fine Bonapartists'.

François Ducray-Duminil (Hugo spells him 'Duchray'), author of tearful, wildly popular sentimental novels around 1800. The volumes lying about the garret are the reading-room romances that also gave Jondrette's daughters their high-flown names.
French for rabble, scum. Hugo calls Jondrette's 'everybody is canaille!' a variant of Solomon's 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity' (Ecclesiastes): the cynic's version of the preacher's despair.

A hackney cab hired in the street, named after the Hôtel Saint-Fiacre where the first cab stand stood. Arriving in one marks a visitor as comfortably off; hence Jondrette's 'He is Rothschild', the name of the great banking family.
quote: He is coming in a fiacre.

term: 'I suppress the liberty of the press'
text: Jondrette's joke when his wife protests. Charles X's attempt to muzzle the press by decree was one of the July Ordinances of 1830 that brought down his throne; the phrase had become a catchword for tyranny.
quote: I suppress the liberty of the press.

text: François-Joseph Talma (died 1826) was the great tragic actor of the Empire, Napoleon's favourite; Mademoiselle Mars was the leading comic actress of the Comédie-Française. Jondrette, posing as the actor Fabantou, claims Talma as his teacher and Mars as his friend.
quote: I am a pupil of Talma!

text: Célimène and Elmire are heroines of Molière (The Misanthrope, Tartuffe), roles Mademoiselle Mars made famous; Belisarius was the Byzantine general said to have ended as a blind beggar. Jondrette casts himself as the ruined old soldier begging from the actress.
quote: Elmire would bestow alms on Bélisaire!

term: Cab tariff: two francs an hour
text: Paris cabs had fixed rates; by the hour, cheaper by the trip. Two francs was a day's pay for many workers. Marius, with sixteen sous in his pocket after giving away his five francs, cannot pay in advance, and the driver whistles and leaves.

The tune of a comic song about Jacques de la Palice, whose verses state the absurdly obvious ('a quarter of an hour before his death, he was still alive'). The cabman's whistling is a mocking dismissal.

A prison in the Marais, in the old town house of the dukes of La Force, used from the Revolution for debtors and criminals awaiting trial. The 'Fosse-aux-Lions', the Lions' Den, was its yard for the most dangerous inmates.
quote: he was discussed at La Force in the Fosse-aux-Lions

text: The proverbially rich king of ancient Lydia. Jondrette's name for the old gentleman shows how he sees him: not as a benefactor but as a fortune walking into reach.

The poor of Paris heated and cooked with charcoal bought by the bushel and burned in a brazier, a portable iron pan. Two bushels for thirty sous is an odd extravagance in a household that has just doused its fire to look poor.

Latin: 'Alone with one alone, in a remote place, they will not be thought to be saying the Lord's Prayer', an old moralist's saying about suspicious meetings. Hugo uses it for the two men talking in the snow behind the wall.
Thieves' slang: 'balles' were francs. The man in the snow means the job is worth five hundred francs a head, against a risk of five to ten years.

One of the boulevard theatres on the Boulevard du Temple, the 'Boulevard of Crime', famous for melodrama full of murders and rescues. The two plotters chat about last night's melodrama while planning a real one.
Hapgood's rendering of 'coups-de-poing': small pocket pistols, short-barrelled and meant for close range, the kind a police officer could carry unseen.
The house on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital is named after a former owner, which is why the inspector, holding Marius's key, mutters 'Former property of Gorbeau': he knows the building well.
Charles X, last Bourbon king of France, reigned 1824–30 and was overthrown in the July Revolution. To dine like him is to dine like a king; by 1832 he is a king in exile.
quote: You shall dine like Charles the Tenth

term: 'Nos amours ont duré toute une semaine'
text: 'Our love lasted a whole week, but how short are the moments of happiness! Adoring each other for eight days, was it worth the trouble?' A sentimental song of the day the girl sings to Marius's mirror; the second, 'You leave me to go to glory', is another romance of parted lovers.
quote: Nos amours ont duré toute une semaine

text: Diogenes the Cynic was said to search Athens with a lantern for an honest man; Cartouche was the notorious Paris robber chief broken on the wheel in 1721. A thieves' dark-lantern is Diogenes's lamp put to the opposite use.

The popular name ('the Mire') for the Port-Royal maternity hospital and dispensary near the Gorbeau quarter, where the poor went for free treatment. Jondrette's story is that the elder girl has taken her sister there.

A Jacobin was a radical of the 1790s, and by extension any republican; a 'bousingot' was a young republican hothead of the early 1830s, known by his varnished sailor's hat. Jondrette protests he is neither, flattering his visitor's supposed respectability.
quote: I am not Jacobin, sir, I am not a bousingot.

text: The French gave presents (étrennes) on New Year's Day, and making the fancy cardboard boxes for sweets and gifts was a small trade open to poor girls. Jondrette claims he meant to apprentice his daughters to it.
quote: the making of boxes for New Year’s gifts

text: Gold twenty-franc pieces struck under Louis-Philippe, the king since 1830, nicknamed after him as earlier coins were called louis or napoleons. The four the visitor lays down are eighty francs, two years' rent for the garret, which lets for forty francs a year.

Jacques-Louis David, the great painter of the Revolution and the Empire, died in exile at Brussels in 1825 after the Restoration banished the regicides. Claiming the daub is 'by David' is Thénardier's absurd attempt to put a price on a tavern signboard.
The men with blackened faces: Hugo calls them 'fumistes', stove-and-chimney workers, whose trade left them sooty. Soot was the cheap mask of the barrière bandit.

Cellini was the Renaissance goldsmith and sculptor; François Villon the fifteenth-century poet who was also a thief. Hugo's point: the galleys hold artists as fine as these, like the convict who can hollow out a sou to hide a watch-spring saw.
quote: There are Benvenuto Cellinis in the galleys

text: Frederick the Great of Prussia reviewed his drilled regiments at Potsdam with a famously cold and complete eye. Javert names each ruffian as he passes them in review, like a general who knows every soldier.
quote: a glance of a Frederick II at a Potsdam parade

text: Two Paris prisons for women. Saint-Lazare, an old leper-house in the Faubourg Saint-Denis, held prostitutes and women awaiting trial; the Madelonettes, a former convent for repentant women in the Marais, held others. With the father at La Force, the whole family is now behind bars.

A nonsense song, 'King Clog-chop went a-hunting, a-hunting for crows', sung by the gamin as he goes. It sets the tone of the scene: a child told where his whole family is jailed answers 'Ah!' and walks off singing.
